extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and USPTO examiners handling PCT (international) applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and mandatory rules for handling PCT international applications: excusing delays, rectification of obvious mistakes, International Searching Authority roles and procedures, search/written-opinion content, and timing/deadlines for searches, demands, and national stage entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excuse for delay or loss in the mail (PCT Rule 82)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay or loss in the mail shall be excused when it is proven to the satisfaction of the receiving Office that the concerned letter or document was mailed at least five days before the expiration of the time limit by registered air mail or, where surface mail would normally arrive within two days of mailing, by registered surface mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT Rule 82 provides detailed provisions; the provisions can excuse failure to meet a time limit for up to six months after the expiration of the time limit provided the document was mailed at least five days before expiry. Evidence is required to satisfy the Office, and a substitute document must be filed promptly (see Rule 82.1(b) and (c)). Examples include mail interruptions due to strike. The mailing method and timing are essential to take advantage of the excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excuse for delays due to interruption of mail or electronic communications (PCT Rule 82 quater/Administrative Instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special provisions apply to excuse delays and extend time limits due to a general disruption experienced by an office or authority (war, revolution, civil disorder, strike, natural calamity, epidemic, general unavailability of electronic communications services or other like reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A delay may be excused where the interested party establishes that an outage affected a widespread geographical area, was unexpected/unforeseen, and no alternative means of communication was available. See PCT Rule 82 quater and PCT Administrative Instruction Section 111 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of periods expiring on non-working days (PCT Rule 80.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: See PCT Rule 80.5 for guidance on periods which expire on a non-working day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance is referenced; offices must apply Rule 80.5 when deadlines fall on non-working days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectification of obvious mistakes — entitlement to request (PCT Rule 91.1(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: An obvious mistake in the international application or another document submitted by the applicant may be rectified in accordance with this Rule if the applicant so requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests can be submitted by the applicant to the competent authority; the rectification process requires authorization (see Rule 91.1(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent authority allocation for rectification (Rule 91.1(b) / summary A–D)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rectification of a mistake shall be subject to authorization by the 'competent authority': (i) mistakes in the request — receiving Office; (ii) mistakes in description/claims/drawings or correction thereof — International Searching Authority unless IPEA is competent; (iii) mistakes in description/claims/drawings or in amendment under Article 19 or 34 where demand for international preliminary examination filed and IPEA competent — International Preliminary Examining Authority; (iv) mistakes in other documents submitted to RO, ISA, IPEA or IB (other than abstract or Article 19 amendment) — that Office/Authority/Bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests must be addressed to the authority competent to authorize the rectification. Forms used include PCT/ISA/217 (ISA) and PCT/IPEA/412 (IPEA). The detailed A–D allocation is important for where to file the rectification request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for authorizing rectification of an obvious mistake (Rule 91.1(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The competent authority shall authorize the rectification if, and only if, it is obvious to the competent authority that, as at the applicable date, something else was intended than what appears in the document concerned and that nothing else could have been intended than the proposed rectification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is objective as of the applicable date (see paragraph (f)). The authority must find both that an intention other than the text existed and that no other intention could reasonably be intended. This is a strict 'obviousness to the authority' test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials the competent authority may consider when deciding rectification (Rules 91.1(d)–(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: For mistakes in description/claims/drawings (and corrections/amendments) the competent authority shall only take into account the contents of the description, claims, drawings and, where applicable, the correction or amendment. For mistakes in the request part or documents referred to in (b)(iv), the authority shall only take into account the international application itself and any documents submitted with the request/correction/document, any available priority document, and other documents in the authority's international application file at the applicable date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority documents cannot be used to support obvious mistake corrections to description/claims/drawings. The scope of materials the authority may look at is limited depending on the type of document containing the mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable date for evaluating obviousness of the mistake (Rule 91.1(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicable date for the purposes of determining obviousness is: (i) for a mistake in a part of the international application as filed — the international filing date; (ii) for a mistake in a document other than the international application as filed — the date on which the document was submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This date determines the contemporaneous record the authority must consider in applying the 'obvious to the authority' test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-rectifiable mistakes under Rule 91.1(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mistake shall not be rectifiable if: (i) the mistake lies in the omission of one or more entire elements of the international application referred to in Article 3(2) or one or more entire sheets; (ii) the mistake is in the abstract; (iii) the mistake is in an amendment under Article 19 (unless IPEA competent); or (iv) the mistake is in a priority claim or in a notice correcting/adding a priority claim where rectification would cause a change in the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exclusions prevent using Rule 91 to add omitted whole elements or to alter priority-determining matters; other Rules (e.g., Rules 20.4, 20.5, 26 bis, 38.3) are not affected by this paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invitation to request rectification when authority notices apparent obvious mistake (Rule 91.1(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Receiving Office, ISA, IPEA or International Bureau discovers what appears to be a rectifiable obvious mistake, it may invite the applicant to request rectification under this Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities have discretion to prompt applicants to request rectification; proactive invitations can be issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit and content for requests for rectification (Rule 91.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for rectification shall be submitted to the competent authority within 26 months from the priority date. It shall specify the mistake and the proposed rectification and may, at the applicant's option, contain a brief explanation. Rule 26.4 applies mutatis mutandis as to how the proposed rectification shall be indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 26-month deadline is jurisdictional for Rule 91 requests. Requests must clearly identify the proposed change and may briefly explain; formatting/indication rules follow Rule 26.4 analogously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization, notification, effect and publication of rectification decisions (Rule 91.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The competent authority shall promptly decide whether to authorize or refuse rectification and notify the applicant and the International Bureau. If authorized, the document shall be rectified in accordance with the Administrative Instructions and be effective from the international filing date (for application-as-filed mistakes) or the date the document was submitted (for mistakes in other documents). On refusal, the IB, upon request within two months and payment of a special fee, shall publish the request, reasons for refusal and applicant comments where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authorized, designated Offices that had already started processing/examination prior to notification need not take rectification into account. A designated Office may disregard an authorized rectification if it would not have authorized it itself, but only after giving the applicant reasonable opportunity to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectification effect on designated Offices and right to disregard
rubrics_metrics.description: A rectification authorized under Rule 91 need not be taken into account by any designated Office in which processing or examination started prior to notification of authorization. A designated Office may disregard an authorized rectification only if it finds it would not have authorized the rectification itself, and must give the applicant opportunity to make observations within a reasonable time limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects national/regional Offices' autonomy but requires procedural fairness (opportunity to respond) before disregarding rectifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectification costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Any such rectification is free of charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 91 rectifications do not carry a fee to the applicant for the rectification itself (though publication after refusal requires a special fee to IB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and limits of obvious mistakes (guidance/examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of rectifiable obvious mistakes include linguistic errors, spelling errors and grammatical errors so long as the meaning of the disclosure does not change upon rectification. Changes to chemical or mathematical formulas would not generally be rectifiable unless they would be common knowledge to anyone. A missing chemical formula or missing line of text would not be considered an obvious mistake subject to rectification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate the practical boundary: minor clerical/linguistic errors v. substantive technical content or omissions which are not rectifiable under Rule 91.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Searching Authority (ISA) primary functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Major functions of the ISA include: (1) approving or establishing the title and abstract; (2) considering unity of invention; (3) conducting international and international-type searches and preparing international and international-type search reports and issuing declarations that no international search report will be established; (4) preparing written opinions of the ISA (PCT Rule 43 bis when necessary); and (5) transmitting the international search report and the written opinion to the applicant and the International Bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the core deliverables and responsibilities an ISA must perform for international applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main procedural steps in the ISA
rubrics_metrics.description: The main procedural steps any international application goes through in the ISA are: (1) the making of the international search (PCT Article 15); (2) preparing the international search report (PCT Article 18 and PCT Rule 43); and (3) for applications with filing date on/after Jan 1, 2004, preparing a written opinion of the ISA (PCT Rule 43 bis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these discrete steps clarifies when search reports and written opinions are produced and their sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for establishing international search report and written opinion (PCT Rules 42/43 bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The time limit for establishing the international search report (or a declaration that no report will be established) and written opinion is three months from the receipt of the search copy by the ISA, or nine months from the priority date, whichever expires later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This governs ISA turnaround; applicants and Offices should expect reports or declarations within these statutory periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of the written opinion of the ISA (PCT Rule 43 bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The written opinion shall state whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, to involve an inventive step (to be non-obvious), and to be industrially applicable; and whether the international application complies with the Treaty and Regulations in so far as checked by the ISA. It may also include observations on clarity of claims, description and drawings, and whether claims are fully supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written opinion is an initial, non-binding technical/legal assessment that informs applicants and (if demanded) the IPEA; it may invite a written reply and amendments where appropriate. It also contains notification relevant to making a demand for international preliminary examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the ISA may declare no international search report will be established (PCT Article 17(2)(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the ISA considers the application relates to subject matter it is not required under the Regulations to search, or that the description/claims/drawings fail to comply with prescribed requirements to such an extent that a meaningful search could not be carried out, the ISA shall declare that no international search report will be established and notify applicant and IB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only certain claims are affected, the ISR shall so indicate for those claims and be established for other claims. This is the mechanism for partial or total non-establishment of an ISR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant prior art for the international search (PCT Rule 33)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant prior art consists of everything made available to the public anywhere in the world by means of written disclosure (including drawings and other illustrations) and capable of assisting in determining novelty and inventive step, provided the making available occurred prior to the international filing date. Written disclosures that refer to non-written means (oral, use, exhibition) shall be mentioned separately with the date. Published applications or patents whose publication date is same as or later than, but whose filing date or claimed priority date is earlier than, the international filing date, shall be specially mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISAs must search broadly across written disclosures prior to the filing date and flag disclosures that involve or refer to other means of public availability; certain documents with later publication but earlier filing/priority merit special mention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention and additional search fees (PCT Article 17(3)/Rule 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the ISA considers the application does not comply with unity of invention, it shall invite the applicant to pay additional fees. The ISA will establish the international search report for the invention first mentioned in the claims ('main invention') and, provided required additional fees are paid within the prescribed time, for other inventions for which fees were paid. National law may treat unsearched parts as withdrawn unless a special fee is paid to the national Office of that State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must choose whether to pay additional search fees to have additional inventions searched; failure to pay can have national effects (withdrawal in particular States) and may require payment of special national fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary International Search (SIS) availability (PCT Rule 45 bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: At any time prior to the expiration of 22 months from the priority date, the applicant can request one or more supplementary international searches each to be carried out by an ISA other than the ISA that carried out the main international search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SIS can be used to obtain additional search coverage from other ISAs; timing (before 22 months) is mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadline for filing a demand for international preliminary examination (PCT Rule 54)
rubrics_metrics.description: A demand for international preliminary examination must be filed prior to the expiration of whichever period expires later: (A) three months from transmittal of the international search report and written opinion to the applicant; or (B) 22 months from the priority date. Otherwise the demand is considered as not submitted. To take advantage of national phase entry time limits of at least 30 months in all States, it may be necessary to file a demand before the expiration of 19 months from the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should note the two alternative cut-offs and the practical 19-month consideration when national phase timings are a concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: National stage entry time limits following PCT Chapters I & II (PCT Articles 22 and 39)
rubrics_metrics.description: National stage requirements are due not later than 30 months from the priority date if no demand has been filed (Article 22(1)). For Chapter II (where a demand was filed prior to the 19th month), Article 39 applies and national stage filing under Article 39(a) is 30 months from the priority date, although national law may fix later time limits. Some Contracting States had not adopted the amended 30-month period at the time of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must consult current WIPO lists of national/regional time limits (www.wipo.int/pct/en/texts/time_limits.html) since some States' national laws may differ; earlier transitional 20-month rules and country exceptions may apply.
